title: The Maldives Plans to Offer Residency to the World’s Ultra Rich – And Create Islands From Scratch to Do It
content:
Once an isolated haven for scuba divers searching for technicolor marine life, the shallow turquoise waters of the Noonu Atoll in the Maldives are in the midst of a makeover.

A fleet of dumper trucks, excavators, forklifts, and cranes has moved into the habitat for protected parrot fish and nurse sharks to sculpt 25 artificial islands and islets from over six million cubic metres of sand dredged from the seabed. 

Known as Project Ayla, the $790 million private development will host over 70 luxury dwellings and represents the vanguard of a new government strategy to lure the high-net-worth crowd to the debt-saddled nation. 

A view of the main worksite island for Project Ayla in July 2026. CREDIT: Hassan Moosa/Maldives Independent

Yet beyond the plumes of coral-smothering sediment churned up by the dredgers, opposition politicians and transparency advocates are warning of an even murkier threat: the prospect of a new international tax shelter and potential money-laundering hub carved from the ocean floor.
snippet: Once an isolated haven for scuba divers searching for technicolor marine life, the shallow turquoise waters of the Noonu Atoll in the Maldives are in the midst of a makeover.

title: Cocaine Boatmen Are Being Blown Up By US Airstrikes, But The Drugs Keep Flowing From Colombia
content:
First, you hear the high-pitched whine of drones overhead. Next comes the boom of explosions.

“And then in the following days, the sea brings in a jerrycan, pieces of a boat, drugs, people too,” says Alberto, a local businessman living on the Colombian peninsula of La Guajira.

This grim sequence of events has become familiar for those based along this arid strip of desert, whose shores are lapped by a part of the Caribbean Sea that has been the site of some 20 deadly U.S. strikes on speedboats over the past year.

The U.S. military campaign against the alleged “narco-terrorists” manning these vessels, known as Operation Southern Spear, has faded from headline news since the first attack was launched over a year ago on September 2. 

Yet it continues to destroy small boats in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific — with at least 235 dead in some 70 strikes so far — in the face of heavy criticism from legal experts and rights groups, who call it an ineffective program of what are essentially extrajudicial murders.
snippet: First, you hear the high-pitched whine of drones overhead. Next comes the boom of explosions.

title: OCCRP Briefing: Power Plays in Central Asia: State Capture, Weaponized Anti-Corruption, and the Rules of Doing Business
content:
Strong economic growth and modernization hide a less cheerful reality across Central Asia, where autocratic regimes are still using state power to capture assets and silence dissent.

Kyrgyzstan reports a strong growth of nearly 11% per year. But as OCCRP journalist Eldiyar Arykbaev noted in this briefing, "the devil is in the details.” This growth comes from gold exports and from the country’s role as a trade middleman between China and Russia, which also helps keep the Russian war economy afloat through sanctions evasion. 

“You won’t see that this economic growth had a positive effect on ordinary people,” Arykbaev said. “There is a very thin layer of people who are winning because of this economic growth: people close to the state, in the president’s circles, and in construction projects funded by the state.”

Leila Nazgül Seiitbek, director of Freedom for Eurasia, explained that Kyrgyz business owners are frequently accused of corruption in order to expropriate their assets — a practice known as “kusturizatsiya,” derived from the Kyrgyz word for "vomiting.”
snippet: Strong economic growth and modernization hide a less cheerful reality across Central Asia, where autocratic regimes are still using state power to capture assets and silence dissent.
